Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> In Focus | Relationships Food For Thought: Ebo Whyte explains the risks male benefactors face when having affairs with female beneficiaries Source : Kareen Tei 5 November 2026 5:19pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Helping a woman through difficult times, receiving her affection and enjoying her appreciation may seem like the beginning of a love story, but renowned Ghanaian playwright and marriage counsellor Uncle Ebo Whyte says men must be careful not to confuse gratitude with romantic feelings.
Sharing his Food for Thought on Joy FM's Super Morning Show on Thursday, November 5, a daily segment on the show, the 72-year-old playwright unpacked two common relationship mistakes men make, explaining how they sometimes mistake a woman's gratitude for love and their own desire to protect and provide for her for genuine romantic feelings.
According to Uncle Ebo, two common mistakes often lead men into relationships under the wrong assumptions: confusing a woman's appreciation for romantic affection and mistaking their own protective instincts for love.
He explained that when a man offers support to a woman going through difficult circumstances, she may naturally respond with kindness, sweetness, and appreciation. However, such gestures do not necessarily mean she has romantic feelings for him.
"When a man is helping a woman, she cannot help but respond with gratitude, sweetness and charm. Unfortunately, a lot of men mistake that for love," he said.
He noted that men sometimes interpret a woman's respectful and accommodating attitude as a sign of romantic interest without considering that her behaviour may simply be an expression of gratitude for the assistance she receives.
He explained that seeing a woman in distress can awaken a man's protective instincts, making him feel responsible for her welfare, happiness, and security.
"A dame in distress calls forth the masculine in a man," he said.
According to him, this desire to protect and provide can become so strong that a man begins to interpret his own sense of responsibility as romantic love.
He explained that when a man combines these feelings with the woman's expressions of gratitude, he may convince himself that the affection is mutual and consequently push the relationship beyond the boundaries of assistance and friendship.
"When these two mistakes come together, that is, when the man is charmed by her sweetness and gratitude and thinks that is evidence of her love for him, and when he responds to his own feelings of protection and care for her and convinces himself that it means he loves her, he is likely to take the relationship across the line into amorous territory," he explained.
Uncle Ebo further examined how the dynamics between a man and a woman can change when a relationship that began with assistance and gratitude develops into a romantic and sexual involvement.
He suggested that before romance enters the picture, a woman receiving help may feel particularly appreciative and accommodating because she recognises the man's kindness and does not necessarily see herself as having any claim over him.
According to him, the woman may begin to expect the man's time, attention, and affection, just as she would in any other romantic relationship.
"She now feels that she has a claim to his time and attention. And when she is not getting them, she will find ways to show her displeasure, and most men are caught off guard by that," he said.
He explained that some men struggle with this transition because they continue to expect the same level of gratitude and patience that characterised the relationship when they were primarily helping the women.
For Uncle Ebo, this is where men must recognise that being a benefactor and being a romantic partner are two entirely different roles.
"If you want a romantic relationship with a girl, you must understand that you are in a very different game from the one you had when you were her benefactor," he advised.
He stressed that a man who chooses to pursue a romantic relationship must be prepared to fulfil the expectations that come with being a partner rather than relying on the kindness and assistance he offered in the past.
Helping a woman should not be mistaken for winning her heart
Despite his caution to men, Uncle Ebo was careful to clarify that his message was not an argument against helping women or people experiencing difficult circumstances.
He described helping those in need as one of life's most rewarding experiences, emphasising that kindness and generosity remain valuable regardless of whether they lead to romantic relationships.
His central message was that men must learn to separate genuine romantic feelings from the satisfaction that comes with helping someone and receiving appreciation in return.
Ultimately, his reflection raises an important lesson about relationships: kindness should not be treated as a guarantee of romantic affection, and gratitude should not automatically be interpreted as love.
For men seeking meaningful relationships, understanding the difference could save them from entering romantic commitments based on assumptions rather than genuine emotional connection.
As he rounded off his presentation, Uncle Ebo encouraged men to learn from the experiences of others rather than wait until they make the same mistakes.
"Only a fool learns only from his own mistakes. The wise learn from the experiences of others."
